clue.text: They're no choice persons, we are told

definitions.text: They're no choice persons, we are told

parts.words: They're no choice persons, we are told
parts.note: plays on the proverb that those who ask for alms cannot be choosers, so the people we are told have no choice are the needy askers

explanation.surface: A remark that certain people are unremarkable, according to hearsay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No choice persons' reads as 'not select people', but it points to the proverb 'beggars can't be choosers'; 'we are told' is the proverb being quoted.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying holds that people who ask for charity cannot pick and choose what they are given.

clue.text: Dress up just for a game

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word for dress is read from bottom to top

parts.note: garb means dress or clothing

explanation.surface: Someone dresses up simply to play a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dress up' looks like one phrase about costume, but 'up' turns GARB round in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Brag is an old British card game, an ancestor of poker.

clue.text: Sporting birds, in the main

parts.note: a main is a series of cockfights, so birds sporting in the main are fighting fowl rather than seabirds

explanation.surface: Birds that play about out at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' suggests the open sea, but a main is also a match of cockfights, where bred fighting birds compete.
explanation.definitionFit: Fighting cocks are birds bred for the sport of cockfighting.

clue.text: They give way to married people

definitions.text: They give way to married people

parts.words: They give way to married people
parts.note: the passages down a church give a way through to the altar for those about to wed

explanation.surface: Things that yield to couples who have wed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give way' suggests yielding, but here it means providing a way: the walkways in a church lead brides and grooms up to be married.
explanation.definitionFit: Church walkways between pews are where wedding processions walk.

clue.text: The cricketer's mistake

parts.note: a fielding position near the batsman in cricket shares its name with a small error

explanation.surface: An error made by a cricket player.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as an error by a player; the word is also the name of the cricket fielder standing beside the wicketkeeper.
explanation.definitionFit: A small blunder is called this, and so is a close catching fielder in cricket.

clue.text: Their meetings are noisy

parts.note: the brass plates of a drum kit clash loudly whenever they meet

explanation.surface: A group whose gatherings are always loud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meetings' suggests people gathering, but it is two brass discs struck together.
explanation.definitionFit: Orchestral percussion plates are clashed together to make a loud crash.

clue.text: What King Edward made?

parts.note: Edward the Confessor earned his title by his piety, so what he made was an admission of sins

explanation.surface: A question about what a king produced.
explanation.walkthrough: King Edward the Confessor, who reigned in England before 1066, took his name from his religious devotion.
explanation.definitionFit: An admission of sins to a priest is what a confessor makes.

clue.text: Figure of speech previously encountered-we hear

indicators.note: signals that the phrase is spoken and the answer sounds like it

parts.note: met afore, old-fashioned for met before, means previously encountered

explanation.surface: Someone recognises an expression they have heard before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Met afore' (met before, in dialect) said out loud sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A metaphor is a figure of speech describing one thing as another.

clue.text: Call for a non-stop performance in London ?:

definitions.text: Call for a non-stop performance in London

parts.words: Call for a non-stop performance in London
parts.note: a shout urging actors to keep going is also the name of a London district

explanation.surface: A demand for a continuous show in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The call is 'Act on!', telling performers to continue; Acton is a district of west London.
explanation.definitionFit: A district of west London whose name splits into a stage instruction to keep acting.

clue.text: Meat from the Argentine?

parts.note: argent is the heraldic word for silver, so meat from the argent side is a cut of beef

explanation.surface: Beef imported from Argentina.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Argentine' suggests Argentina and its beef, but argent means silver, so this is a silver side: a British cut of beef from the hindquarter.
explanation.definitionFit: Silverside is a joint of beef cut from the outside of the thigh.

clue.text: People get taken in by it

definitions.text: People get taken in by it

parts.words: People get taken in by it
parts.note: taken in means let in, not deceived: an entry ticket lets people in

explanation.surface: A trick that fools people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken in' suggests being fooled, but it means being let inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Being allowed entry to a place is gaining entrance.

clue.text: The ultimate in make-up

parts.note: make up here means add up, so the ultimate figure is the sum

explanation.surface: The finest cosmetics available.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make-up' suggests cosmetics, but figures make up a sum, and the final figure is the whole.
explanation.definitionFit: A sum is the final figure that the numbers add up to.

clue.text: He's brought to account painfully.

definitions.note: the definition is an adverb for hurting, while the answer is the verb hurts

indicators.note: signals that one piece is placed after the other, the second joined on to the first

parts.note: the letters of he's, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A man is held to account in a way that hurts.
explanation.definitionFit: To throb with discomfort is to hurt painfully.

clue.text: We'll have to trust 'em like the old-time coppers

definitions.text: We'll have to trust 'em like the old-time coppers

parts.words: We'll have to trust 'em like the old-time coppers
parts.note: the coppers are coins, not police: the new decimal coins must be trusted as the old pennies were

explanation.surface: We must trust the police as people once did.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coppers' suggests police officers, but it is British slang for low-value bronze coins; decimal coins replaced the old pennies in 1971.
explanation.definitionFit: Decimal coins introduced in Britain in 1971 replaced the old penny coins.

clue.text: People in this business hold acting appointments

definitions.text: People in this business hold acting appointments

parts.words: People in this business hold acting appointments
parts.note: acting appointments sound like temporary posts, but here they are roles on the stage

explanation.surface: Staff in a firm hold temporary positions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Acting appointments' usually means stand-in posts; here they are stage engagements.
explanation.definitionFit: The stage business, as an adjective, describes the world of actors.

clue.text: This should be extremely comforting to the timorous

definitions.text: This should be extremely comforting to the timorous

parts.words: This should be extremely comforting to the timorous
parts.note: timid people get cold feet, and extremely means at the body's extremities

explanation.surface: Something that greatly reassures nervous people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' is read as 'to the extremities', and the timorous have cold feet.
explanation.definitionFit: A heated pad or bottle keeps the feet from getting cold.

clue.text: Cut out for equestrian exercise

definitions.meaning: a leisurely ride out on a horse

explanation.surface: Someone is cut out for horse riding.
explanation.definitionFit: To chop roughly is to cut; an ordinary ride on horseback is also called this.

clue.text: Poor sleepers were glad-of these

parts.note: poor sleepers suggests insomniacs, but it means penniless people needing cheap beds

explanation.surface: Insomniacs were grateful for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor sleepers' sounds like people who sleep badly; it means poor people who sleep in cheap lodgings.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheap lodging houses gave beds to the destitute.

clue.text: Capital rubber washer

parts.note: capital means excellent, and the rubber is someone who rubs and washes hair

explanation.surface: A fine rubber ring for plumbing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubber washer' suggests a plumbing part; it is a person who rubs and washes heads, and 'capital' (excellent) also hints at the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairdresser's assistant who rubs soap into and rinses hair.

clue.text: Back in hospital ?

parts.note: a ward at the rear of a hospital is literally a back one

explanation.surface: Someone has returned to hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back in hospital' sounds like readmission; split, the answer is a ward at the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Towards the rear, or backwards, as a ward at the back would be.

clue.text: Obtains-ten perhaps, but no X from: this

indicators.note: suggests the letters might be put together some other way

explanation.surface: Someone gets ten votes, yet no cross is marked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' shuffles OBTAINS and TEN; X is the cross a voter marks, and withholding it is declining to vote.
explanation.definitionFit: Declining to vote means placing no cross on the ballot.

clue.text: A shaggy-dog story can hardly be a "— and unconvincing narrative"

definitions.text: A shaggy-dog story can hardly be a "— and unconvincing narrative"

parts.words: A shaggy-dog story can hardly be a "— and unconvincing narrative"
parts.note: completes Gilbert's phrase from The Mikado, with a joke that a shaggy dog is hairy rather than hairless

explanation.surface: A rambling joke cannot be dismissed as a feeble tale.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is 'merely corroborative detail, intended to give artistic verisimilitude to an otherwise bald and unconvincing narrative' from The Mikado; a shaggy dog is the opposite of hairless.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain and unadorned, as well as lacking hair, which a shaggy dog never is.

clue.text: Take-off instruction ?

parts.note: a take-off can be an imitation, or a plane leaving the ground: both are taught by instruction

explanation.surface: An order given to a pilot before flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take-off instruction' sounds like a control-tower command; it is teaching, such as a flying class.
explanation.definitionFit: A period of instruction is a class or tutorial.

clue.text: Clubman doing, the rounds?

parts.note: the club is a service club named for meeting in rotation, so its member goes round

explanation.surface: A golfer playing his rounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubman' and 'rounds' suggest golf; the Rotary Club was named for its members hosting meetings in rotation.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the Rotary service club.

clue.text: It would be advantageous to do her a turn.

indicators.note: doing her a turn means writing her name the other way round

parts.note: an asset is something advantageous to have

explanation.surface: Doing a woman a favour would pay off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do her a turn' sounds like doing her a favour; it means reversing her name, which gives ASSET.
explanation.definitionFit: Tessa is a woman's name, so it stands for a female 'her'.

clue.text: Play-time to the musician

parts.note: playtime suggests a school break, but for a musician the time a piece is played at is its speed

explanation.surface: A break for a performer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play-time' suggests a break, but it is the time, or speed, at which music is played.
explanation.definitionFit: The speed at which a piece of music is played.

clue.text: With, this covering one is still liable to exposure

definitions.text: With, this covering one is still liable to exposure

parts.words: With, this covering one is still liable to exposure
parts.note: a still is a photograph, and exposure is light reaching the sensitive coating in a camera

explanation.surface: Even wearing this, a person can still catch cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covering' and 'exposure' suggest clothing and cold; a still is a photograph, made by exposing a coated strip in a camera.
explanation.definitionFit: The light-sensitive coated strip in a camera, exposed to make a photograph.

clue.text: Become engaged in some shady business

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the letters of these words

explanation.surface: Someone gets involved in a dodgy deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' points inside 'some shady'; gear teeth that engage are said to mesh.
explanation.definitionFit: Gear teeth that interlock are said to engage.

clue.text: What Cicero said was Greek to him

definitions.text: What Cicero said was Greek to him

parts.words: What Cicero said was Greek to him
parts.note: in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar a conspirator reports that Cicero spoke Greek, and 'it was Greek to me'

explanation.surface: Someone could not understand the Roman orator.
explanation.walkthrough: In Julius Caesar the conspirator Casca says of Cicero's speech, 'for mine own part, it was Greek to me', literally true as Cicero spoke Greek.
explanation.definitionFit: The conspirator in Shakespeare's play who coined the phrase about not understanding.

clue.text: A girl puts on weight in town

indicators.note: signals that one piece is followed by the other, the girl taking on weight

parts.note: a maid is a girl
a stone is a British weight of fourteen pounds

explanation.surface: A young woman gains weight while in town.
explanation.walkthrough: A stone is a British unit of weight, 14 pounds. Maidstone is the county town of Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: Maidstone is a large town in Kent, south-east England.

clue.text: Hero-worship got him into deep water

definitions.text: Hero-worship got him into deep water

parts.words: Hero-worship got him into deep water
parts.note: Hero was a priestess, and her lover swam the Hellespont nightly to reach her

explanation.surface: Admiring someone too much landed a man in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hero-worship' suggests idolising; in Greek legend the youth loved Hero and swam the Hellespont to her, drowning in the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The lover in the Greek legend of Hero who swam the strait to her.

clue.text: Ruler gets on in one walk of life

indicators.note: the little word on goes inside the word for walk

parts.note: to march is to walk in step

explanation.surface: A leader prospers in a particular line of work.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a career success in one line of work; 'one walk of life' is a link phrase here, and 'gets ... in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A sovereign such as a king or queen rules a country.
